meta.title: Who really said "Dancing is a perpendicular expression of a horizontal desire"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Frost. The line first appears in the New Statesman, 23 March 1962, already credited to George Bernard Shaw and already without a source.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Dancing is a perpendicular expression of a horizontal desire'?
meta.ogDescription: No Frost source exists. The line surfaces in the New Statesman on 23 March 1962, credited to a Shaw who had been dead more than a decade, with no citation.

answer.label: Not Robert Frost — origin unresolved
answer.authorDates: Earliest known appearance 1962 · credited there, without a source, to George Bernard Shaw
answer.sourceLine: There is no Frost source — no poem, no letter, no lecture, no reported remark. The saying’s earliest known appearance anywhere is George Melly’s New Statesman article of 23 March 1962, where it is already secondhand: something ‘Shaw called’ dancing, offered with no citation, and Shaw had been dead since 1950. Quote Investigator ↗ names Shaw the leading candidate on that thin basis and rules the Frost, Churchill and Wilde credits unconvincing. The Frost version does not enter its record until 2014.

source.heading: The paper trail

source.excerpt: I have spent a certain amount of time lately watching people in London dance in the various new ways. I report what went on in three very different places where my fellow countrymen and women had come together to give what Shaw called ‘a perpendicular expression of a horizontal desire’.
trail: 23 March 1962 — the first sighting. The jazz singer and critic George Melly, writing on the London dance craze in the New Statesman, describes people gathering to give ‘what Shaw called a perpendicular expression of a horizontal desire.’ No citation; and Shaw’s death in 1950 preceded the article by more than a decade. Quote Investigator calls this the earliest evidence it has found ↗.

1972 — syndication does the rest. Ann Landers answered a reader with a ‘vertical expression of a horizontal idea’ variant, putting the saying into hundreds of American papers — but it was already circulating. Barry Popik’s Big Apple entry ↗ tracks the same spread and states flatly that there is no documentary evidence Wilde or Frost ever said it.

Wikiquote files it under ‘Attributed’ — to Shaw, not to Frost. The George Bernard Shaw page ↗ lists the line in its Attributed section with the bare note ‘Attributed by George Melly in 1962’. The Robert Frost page ↗ does not carry it at all, in any wording.

2014 — Frost’s name arrives, very late. The earliest Frost credit in Quote Investigator’s chronology is a writing manual, Mastering the Craft of Writing by Stephen Wilbers, which introduces the line with ‘Here’s how the poet gave it to us.’ QI rules the Frost, Churchill and Wilde attributions unconvincing ↗.
source.excerptNote: This is the earliest appearance of the saying that anyone has located — and note what it already is: a report, not a coinage. Melly hands the line to Shaw and supplies no source. Transcribed by Quote Investigator from the New Statesman of 23 March 1962.

source.rightsNote: No copyright status can be responsibly asserted, because the saying has no identified author and no identified first work. The oldest text demonstrably containing it is George Melly’s New Statesman article of 23 March 1962 — itself in copyright, and quoting the line as somebody else’s. Nothing ties the wording to any pre-1931 publication, and nothing ties it to Robert Frost. This is not legal advice.

author.name: George Bernard Shaw
author.heading: Why the trail stops at Shaw
author.metaLine: 1856–1950 · Irish playwright, critic and Nobel laureate in Literature
author.bio: George Bernard Shaw wrote Arms and the Man (1894), Man and Superman (1902), Pygmalion (1913) and Saint Joan (1923), took the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1925 and an Academy Award for the Pygmalion screenplay in 1938 — the kind of range that makes almost any sharp epigram sound plausible in his voice. He is the only name in this story with even a foothold in the documents: his is the name George Melly used in 1962, the earliest sighting anyone has found. But Shaw had been dead more than a decade by then, the line is not in his published writings, and Quote Investigator ↗ is explicit that the evidence for him is poor.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: Four famous names have been attached to this sentence, plus one advice columnist who merely repeated it. Not one of the four has a source behind them — and the poet has the thinnest claim of all, arriving more than half a century after the line was already in print.

items.who: Robert Frost — nothing connects him to it
items.why: Frost died in January 1963, so he was still alive when the saying first surfaced in print in March 1962 — and it was credited to somebody else. The earliest Frost credit in Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗ is a 2014 writing manual, and QI calls the attribution unconvincing. Aggregators such as Quotes.net ↗ still print it under his name with no source line at all.

items.who: George Bernard Shaw — leading candidate, unproven
items.why: Shaw is where most of the internet lands, and he is Quote Investigator’s leading candidate for one reason only: his is the name in the earliest citation. QI is blunt that ‘this evidence was poor.’ The line does not appear in Shaw’s published writings, and Wikiquote files it under Attributed ↗, sourced to nothing but Melly’s 1962 mention.

Wilde died in 1900. A 1984 book on erotic and bawdy language credited him with ‘a vertical expression of a horizontal urge’; Quote Investigator ↗ logs that instance in its chronology and rules the Wilde attribution unconvincing.

A column in The Indianapolis Star of 11 January 1999 assigned the line to Churchill as ‘the vertical expression of a horizontal urge.’ It is simply the next famous name in the queue, and QI finds it no better supported ↗ than the Wilde or Frost credits.

Her syndicated column of 27 October 1972 used the ‘vertical expression of a horizontal idea’ form while defending close dancing. Barry Popik ↗ and Quote Investigator both treat this as a spreading event, not an origin — the saying was already a decade into print.

misattribution.truthLine: The one thing the record actually shows: the sentence first appears in George Melly’s New Statesman piece of 23 March 1962, already credited to Shaw and already without a source. Everything after that — Johar, Landers, Wilde, Churchill, Frost — is repetition with a new name on it. See the full chronology ↗.

context.heading: An orphan epigram, adopted repeatedly
lead: The joke is older in shape than in wording. Quote Investigator’s chronology opens with two near-misses that have nothing to do with dancing: a 1914 London magazine calling New York’s Woolworth and Singer towers ‘the perpendicular expression for the horizontal growth of American fortunes,’ and a 1921 music lecture contrasting the ‘perpendicular and horizontal movements of musical expression.’ The antithesis was in the air. The dance version, when it finally lands in 1962, arrives fully formed and already secondhand — Melly is reporting the line, not claiming it, and the man he credits cannot be asked.

Then it mutates, which is the tell. Perpendicular becomes vertical; desire becomes idea, then urge, then wish; expression becomes manifestation. A Delhi weekly gave it to the Indian actor I. S. Johar in 1966; a London novel used ‘vertical expressors of horizontal desires’ in 1968; a Vermont state legislator deployed it against television dancing in 1974; and a Massachusetts columnist in 1975 remembered a University of Massachusetts botanist delivering it to generations of students. That churn is the signature of an orphan saying: everybody has heard it, everybody assigns it to whichever wit they most admire, and nobody can produce the page.
context.detailsSummary: What Frost really wrote about dancing — and the one lead still open
detailsBody: What Frost actually wrote about dancing. The one Frost couplet on the subject is the two-line poem ‘The Secret Sits’, collected in A Witness Tree (1942): ‘We dance round in a ring and suppose, / But the Secret sits in the middle and knows.’ It sits on his Wikiquote page ↗ among the sourced quotations. The perpendicular line does not appear there at all.

The one loose thread. Quote Investigator flags the actor and writer I. S. Johar as ‘an interesting possibility’ and hopes a future researcher will turn up a precise citation in the Indian film magazine Filmfare. The 1966 instance QI located is itself secondhand — a Delhi weekly quoting Johar — and it comes after the 1962 sighting, so it does not displace it. Until that Filmfare page is found, the honest answer is that nobody knows who said this first.
context.pull: Melly is reporting the line in 1962, not coining it — and the man he credits had been dead more than a decade.

sourcesVerified.claim: Earliest known evidence is the New Statesman of 23 March 1962, where George Melly attributes the saying to George Bernard Shaw with no citation; Shaw's 1950 death preceded the article by more than a decade; the earliest Robert Frost credit is 2014 in Stephen Wilbers's Mastering the Craft of Writing, p. 155; QI concludes the Frost, Churchill and Wilde attributions were unconvincing and that Shaw is the leading candidate on poor evidence. Chronology also includes a 1914 New Age architectural precursor, a 1921 music-lecture precursor, 1966 I. S. Johar via Filmfare, 1968 Anthony Nayman, 1972 Ann Landers, 1973 Irish Times, 1974 Rep. Patrick Harte, 1975 Ray Ethan Torrey, 1984 Oscar Wilde credit, 1999 Winston Churchill credit.

Wikiquote lists 'Dancing is a perpendicular expression of a horizontal desire' under the top-level '== Attributed ==' section of the George Bernard Shaw page, annotated 'Attributed by George Melly in 1962' and citing Quote Investigator; the page gives Shaw's dates as 26 July 1856 - 2 November 1950.

Wikiquote's Robert Frost page contains no instance of the dancing line in any wording (no 'perpendicular'/'horizontal' match) and has no Misattributed or Disputed section; it does carry 'We dance round in a ring and suppose, / But the Secret sits in the middle and knows' ('The Secret Sits') within its A Witness Tree (1942) section.

Barry Popik's Big Apple entry states there is no documentary evidence that Wilde or Frost ever said this, that Shaw was credited in the New Statesman on March 23, 1962 (well after his 1950 death), and that the saying does not appear to be printed in Shaw's writings; it documents further circulation including the 1972 Ann Landers column.
Quotes.net credits 'Dancing is a vertical expression of a horizontal desire' to Robert Frost and provides no source, book, or date for the attribution.

Robert Frost: born 26 March 1874, died 29 January 1963, American, four Pulitzer Prizes for Poetry; collections include A Boy's Will (1913), North of Boston (1914), Mountain Interval (1916), New Hampshire (1923), A Further Range (1936), A Witness Tree (1942). The article contains no mention of dancing or 'horizontal desire'.

George Bernard Shaw: born 26 July 1856, died 2 November 1950, Irish; Nobel Prize in Literature 1925; Academy Award 1938 for the adapted screenplay of Pygmalion; plays include Arms and the Man (1894), Man and Superman (1902), Pygmalion (1913), Saint Joan (1923). The article does not mention dancing or 'horizontal desire'.
George Melly (17 August 1926 - 5 July 2007) was an English jazz and blues singer, critic, writer and lecturer, and the author of Revolt into Style: The Pop Arts in Britain (1970).

American Dialect Society mailing-list post by Garson O'Toole, 8 September 2016, presenting the research: the 1962 New Statesman citation by George Melly reprinted in Revolt into Style (1970), the 1968 Anthony Nayman variant, the 1972 Ann Landers column, and the 1914 New Age architectural precursor.
